dok_rationale: Part (c) requires matching a stated question to the table that can answer it (counts vs. relative frequencies), citing the numbers that settle it, and reasoning about what each club's chosen table conceals from a reader; the choice must be defended against the other table rather than read off, and either table can be argued for.
stem: Two clubs asked the student council for money to run a Saturday session. Each club surveyed \emph{all} of its members: ``Would you attend a Saturday session?'' The table shows every response as a count.\par\smallskip At the council meeting, the \textbf{Robotics club} presented a \textbf{frequency table} (counts) and the \textbf{Chess club} presented a \textbf{relative-frequency table} (percents). Each club chose the table that made its case look best.
first_take: Which club has more interest in a Saturday session --- Chess or Robotics? One sentence and one number.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: How many Robotics members said Yes? Which club has more members, and how many more?

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Build the relative-frequency table: for each club, the percent of its members who said Yes and the percent who said No (nearest whole percent). Which club has the higher percentage saying Yes?

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: The council asks: ``Which club has \textbf{more student interest} in a Saturday session?'' Decide which table --- counts or percents --- answers \emph{that} question, and cite the specific numbers that settle it. Then explain what each club's chosen table \textbf{hides} from a reader: what does the Robotics club's frequency table hide, and what does the Chess club's percent table hide?

answers.a: 27 Robotics members said Yes. Robotics has more members: 45 vs.\ 18, so 27 more.
answers.b: Chess: Yes $15/18 \approx 83\%$, No $3/18 \approx 17\%$. Robotics: Yes $27/45 = 60\%$, No $18/45 = 40\%$. Each row adds to $100\%$. Chess has the higher percentage saying Yes ($83\%$ vs.\ $60\%$).
answers.c: Expected: ``more student interest'' asks \emph{how many students} are interested, so the \textbf{frequency table} answers it: 27 Robotics members said Yes vs.\ 15 Chess members --- 12 more people would show up. (A student who reads the question as ``which club's \emph{members} are more interested'' and picks the percent table, $83\%$ vs.\ $60\%$, earns full credit \emph{if they say that is the question the percents answer}.) What the tables hide: the Robotics club's \textbf{counts} hide the base sizes --- Robotics has 45 members to Chess's 18, so 27 Yes is only $60\%$ of the club and 18 Robotics members said No. The Chess club's \textbf{percents} hide how small the base is --- $83\%$ is 15 people out of only 18; $83\%$ of 18 (15) is fewer students than $60\%$ of 45 (27).

expectedElements.description: Commits to one table and ties the choice to what the council's question asks (how many students vs. what share of a club); either table accepted with that reason
Cites the specific numbers that settle it (27 vs. 15 Yes, or 83\% vs. 60\%)
Says the Robotics frequency table hides that the clubs are different sizes (45 vs. 18), so 27 Yes is only 60\% / 18 said No
Says the Chess percent table hides that 83\% is 15 people out of only 18 (a percent needs its base)

scoringGuide.E: Commits to one table with a reason tied to the council's question, cites the settling numbers, AND names both hides (club sizes behind the counts; the small base behind the percent).
scoringGuide.P: Commits with numbers but names only one hide, OR names both hides but never commits to a table or gives no reason tied to the question, OR the reason is `percents are always fairer' with no link to what was asked.
scoringGuide.I: Says the two tables say the same thing, or picks a table with no numbers, or names no hide.

commonMistakes: `Percents are always better' (or `counts are the real data') with no link to what the council asked
Cites 83\% without ever saying it is 15 people out of 18
Compares 27 Yes to 15 Yes without noting Robotics has 45 members to Chess's 18
Reports 27/45 as `27\%' --- treats a count as a percent

sentence_frames: ``More student interest'' is answered by the \blank[0.9in] table because the question asks \blank[2.2in].
The Chess club's percents hide that \blank[2in]; the Robotics club's counts hide that \blank[2in].

dok_rationale: Converting a frequency table to a relative-frequency table and checking that the percents add to 100 applies one known procedure across four categories with a self-check, no judgment between alternatives.
stem: Suppose 25 students in a class were asked their favorite lunch: Pizza 11, Tacos 8, Salad 4, Other 2. Make the relative-frequency table (nearest whole percent) and check that your percents add to $100\%$. Then write one sentence about the class that a reader could verify from your table.

answers.a: Pizza $11/25 = 44\%$, Tacos $32\%$, Salad $16\%$, Other $8\%$; sum $= 100\%$. Sentence names the variable and a checkable claim, e.g. ``Fewer than half the class (44\%) chose pizza'' or ``Pizza and tacos together make up 76\% of the class.''
